title: Your questions, taken seriously
subtitle: Twelve short sessions for someone who has stepped back from faith or from church: the hurt, the questions, the silence of God, and the older faith underneath what you were handed, with no hurry.
intro: This track is for someone who has stepped back from faith, or from church, or from both. Maybe a church hurt you. Maybe you began taking apart what you were taught and can't tell yet what is left. Maybe God simply went quiet. It has twelve sessions of about ten minutes each, and you can take them a week apart or a month apart. Nothing here asks you to come back to church, to believe by the last session, or to decide anything.

Each session works the same way. You read a few short paragraphs, then open one page on this site and use it, then come back to one question, one thing to do, and one verse. The early sessions stay with the hurt and the questions. The later ones dig for what is older than the church you knew. If you can, take the track with one person you trust. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Your questions, taken seriously. The group is for people who have stepped back from faith or from church, and it can hold people who still believe, people who no longer do, and people who don't know. Many will carry a wound from a church, so the leader's first task is to make the room safe, and the second is to keep the questions honest. Nobody is there to be argued back, and the group sets no deadline on any decision about church or faith, in either direction.

Each person reads the session and opens its page before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what people found, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to eight people is a good size, small enough that each person is heard. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week or once a fortnight, for twelve meetings, and keep the end time you promised. Think before you meet in a church building, because for some people the building itself is hard to walk into, and a living room may be kinder. A leader doesn't need an answer to every question. A leader needs to be trustworthy, patient, and not anxious about where anyone lands.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit in a circle, with the session on a phone or printed for each person. Make three things plain at the first meeting. Anyone may pass on any question. What people say about their own lives stays in the room, unless someone is in danger. And no one will be asked to pray aloud, to come back to church, or to decide anything. Say the part about danger out loud at the start, so that no one is surprised by it later.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse aloud, and a few verses around it when the session opens a chapter of the Bible.
Forty minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Let a silence sit before you fill it.
Ten minutes: what each person noticed in the page the session opened, and anything they would push back on.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt for those who pray, and quiet for everyone else.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Some of the hardest questions in this group will be about the church, and some will be about God. Welcome both. Say what is true in an objection before anything else, and never defend a church or a leader against someone's account of what was done to them. If the page the session opened takes the question up, read that part aloud together. If no one knows the answer, say so, write the question down, and bring it back the next week.

Keep two crowds out of the room: the one that panics when someone takes their faith apart, and the one that cheers them toward the door. Where Christians themselves disagree, say that they do, and let the group see more than one answer. The aim is not to bring anyone back by the twelfth meeting. It is that each person meets the questions, and the faith, as they really are.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Many people in this group will carry harm done in a church or in God's name: a leader who could not be questioned, abuse that was covered up, a family that turned away. When someone tells their story, stop the discussion and listen. Believe them and thank them for saying it. Don't explain, don't correct details, and don't speak up for the church or the person involved, even if you know them. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a leader, a partner or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A crime, and above all harm to a child, belongs with the police and the proper authorities, not with a church to handle quietly. Never ask anyone to meet the person who hurt them, to forgive quickly, or to stay where they are being hurt.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief or sadness that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, a fear of God or of hell that will not let them rest, panic at the thought of walking into a church, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: If a church hurt you
teaching: Many people who step back from faith didn't walk away from God first. They walked away from a church, or they were pushed. It may have been a pastor who couldn't be questioned, abuse that was covered up, a congregation that closed ranks when someone spoke up, or a quieter wound, like being dropped the month you divorced or got sick. If that is part of your story, it comes first here, before any question about belief. Scripture is harder on leaders who harm people than the church that hurt you may ever have been. Through Ezekiel, God says of the shepherds who fed on the flock, “Behold, I am against the shepherds” (Ezekiel 34:10).

The page this session opens says what to do first. If anyone is still in danger, or a crime was done, it belongs with the police, not only with a church. If you are safe, you don't have to decide anything about church this week. Start by telling the truth to one person outside that church who will believe you. The page also draws a line worth keeping. Disappointment is the ordinary cost of living among people who fail, but using God's name to control or silence someone is different in kind. Staying away from the people who did it is not the same as staying away from Christ. If no church hurt you, read on anyway, or go to the next session.

open.label: The church hurt me
open.why: Written for someone a church or its leaders harmed: naming it honestly, reporting what must be reported, and taking time to heal.

also.label: Eight Weeks After the Church Hurt You
also.why: Eight slow weeks: safety first, the Psalms' words for betrayal, and no hurry back through any church door.

sessions.question: If you said what happened to you in a church in one plain sentence, without softening it to spare anyone, what would that sentence be?
sessions.do: Choose one person outside the church that hurt you, a friend, a relative, a counsellor, or a pastor from another church, and tell them plainly what happened. If you can't yet, write it down for your eyes only.

verse.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.

care: If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is one thing a church once gave you that you still miss, if there is one?
discuss: The page separates ordinary disappointment in a church from the use of God's name to control or silence someone. Why does that difference matter?
In Ezekiel, God is not neutral about shepherds who harm the flock. What changes when you hear that God takes the side of the people they hurt?
What would this group need to be for someone a church has hurt to feel safe in it?
group.pray: Those who pray may bring the harm done in God's name to him in plain words, and pray for anyone in the group still carrying it. Others can keep a minute of quiet.

sessions.title: If you're taking it apart
teaching: Some people step back because something cracked: a leader who fell, a church that began to sound like a campaign, a question that got a verse and a warning instead of an answer. Then one loose piece pulls on the next, and everything seems to come down at once. Looking hard at what you were given isn't a sin, and some of it deserves to go. The Bereans were praised because they “examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). But sort as you go. The church culture you were raised in is not the same thing as the faith Christians have confessed for centuries, and you can lose the first without losing the second.

The page this session opens tells the story of King Josiah. When the Book of the Law was found during repairs to the temple, he tore down what had been added and recovered what was older (2 Kings 22 and 23). The page calls that excavation, not demolition. Taking apart can become a place to live, and a heart doesn't stay empty for long. So carry two questions through this track: what has to go, and what you are digging toward. Paul names the foundation that was laid before anyone built on it: “no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

open.label: I'm deconstructing my faith
open.why: Written for someone sorting what they were handed: what deserves to go, what is older underneath, and what to do this week.

sessions.question: Of the things you no longer believe, which belong to the faith itself, and which belong to the package it came in?
sessions.do: Write down what you no longer believe or aren't sure of, one line each. Mark each line by where it belongs: God and Jesus, the Bible, the church and its leaders, politics and culture, or the rules you were raised with. Don't argue with any of it yet.

verse.text: For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is one thing you were taught about God as a child that you now see differently?
discuss: The page names two crowds, one afraid for the person taking their faith apart and one cheering them toward the door. What does each get right, and what does each miss?
Josiah tore down what had been added and recovered something older. How is that different from simply tearing down?
Paul says the foundation is Christ and the rest is what builders added. Which of the things you were taught was a builder's addition?
group.pray: Those who pray may ask for honesty to let go of what was never the faith, and courage to keep what is. Anyone who doesn't pray can sit with the same question in the quiet.

sessions.title: Done with church, not with Jesus?
teaching: Many people who stop going to church never stop praying, and never stop believing that Jesus rose. They drifted, or they left a room that hurt them, and they still love the one the room was named for. The answer this session opens starts there. A faith like that is plainly real, and nobody is asking you back into the room that hurt you. The thing you long for was never the room. Its question is a different one: whether a faith this real was ever meant to be carried alone.

When crowds walked away from Jesus, he asked the Twelve whether they wanted to leave too, and Peter answered, “Lord, to whom would we go?” (John 6:68). He didn't say it alone. He said it beside eleven others who had also decided to stay. The New Testament pictures the church as a body, and a hand on its own isn't a freer hand. None of this is a demand to go back this week. It is a question to hold, gently and for as long as it takes: who knows you well enough to ask how your faith is, and who would you let ask?

open.label: Done with church but not Jesus?
open.why: A short, straight answer for someone who still loves Jesus and can't face a church, with what it asks of you and what it doesn't.

also.label: Can you be a Christian without going to church?
also.why: The same question from the other side: what it means to believe alone, and why a faith built for two or more aches when it runs on one.

sessions.question: What do you miss about belonging to a church, and what would you never want back?
sessions.do: Name one or two believers you trust who had no part in what hurt you. Tell one of them honestly where you are with church and with Jesus, and ask them to pray for you.

verse.text: Simon Peter replied, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

care: If you have been harmed by someone in a church, and were told to forgive and say nothing, what happened to you may have been wrong. Please talk with someone you trust outside that situation. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the best thing a church ever did for you, or for someone you love?
discuss: The answer says many people who leave church never stop believing. Why do you think a church so often fails to notice them leaving?
Peter's answer to Jesus was his own, but he gave it beside eleven others. How can a faith be personal without being solitary?
What would a church have to be for you to want to belong to it, and could any church be that?
group.pray: Those who pray may pray for each person in the group by name, and for the churches that failed them. Anyone who doesn't pray can keep a minute of quiet.

sessions.title: Angry at God
teaching: Some people step back from faith because they are angry with God, and they assume the anger has already put them outside it. The Bible says otherwise. Many of the psalms are laments, honest complaints addressed to God himself, and God kept them in the book his people pray. “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). That is not a polite question. In the book of Job, the man who accused God to his face for chapter after chapter is not the one God rebukes. God rebukes the friends who defended him: “you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (Job 42:7).

The answer this session opens draws a line between two kinds of anger. One walks out. The other stays in the room and says to God's face what it feels, and that is still faith, holding on. Jesus himself cried out from the cross with the first line of a lament: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34). Anger isn't the opposite of faith, the answer says. Walking away in silence is. If you are angry with God, you are allowed to tell him so, in the very words you are afraid to use.

open.label: Is it okay to be angry at God?
open.why: Three short paragraphs on the psalms of complaint, the anger that walks out and the anger that stays, and the cry from the cross.

also.label: Anger at God
also.why: What Scripture says to someone angry with God, Job's protest among it, and passages to pray when your own words run out.

sessions.question: If you told God what you are angry about, in your own words and without softening it, what would you say?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 13 aloud. Then write your own complaint in the same shape: how long, what you need, and only if you can, one line of trust. If you can't write the last part yet, leave it blank.

verse.text: Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him. God is our refuge.

care: If your own suffering does not feel light, you are not failing. Many of the psalms are cries of people for whom it did not feel light either. “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). God kept those prayers in his book. If it is heavy, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Were you ever told that being angry with God was wrong? Who told you, and how?
discuss: Why do you think God kept the angry psalms in the Bible, and not only the grateful ones?
Job's friends defended God and were rebuked, while Job accused him and was not. What does that suggest about the prayers God wants?
The answer separates anger that walks out from anger that stays in the room. Which of the two describes where you are?
group.pray: Those who pray may tell God plainly what they are angry about, aloud or in silence, without tidying it first. Anyone who doesn't pray can name it to themselves in the quiet.

sessions.title: A prayer for when you can't pray
teaching: When faith comes apart, prayer is often the first thing to go quiet. The old words feel false, and new ones don't come. The psalms were written for that. Psalm 42 is the prayer of someone who once led the crowds to the house of God and is now far from it, while people keep asking where his God has gone. “My tears have been my food both day and night, while men ask me all day long, ‘Where is your God?’” (Psalm 42:3). He remembers the singing, and he misses it.

The psalm argues with itself. Its refrain comes back because the hope hasn't caught up with the tears, and even the hope is in the future tense: “I will yet praise Him” (Psalm 42:5). Borrowed words are no failure of faith. When your own words won't come, you can pray words that have held up other people before you, and stop at the line you can't say yet. You aren't pretending to a certainty you don't have. You are letting older words hold you up for a while.

open.label: Pray Psalm 42 slowly
open.why: A worshiper far from the house of God, talking back to his own downcast soul. Choose ‘Pray it slowly’ and it shows one part at a time.

sessions.question: Which line of Psalm 42 could you say honestly today, and which can't you say yet?
sessions.do: Pray Psalm 42 aloud once a day for a week, slowly, and go on into Psalm 43, which finishes the poem. Stop at any line you can't say yet, and leave it there without forcing it.

verse.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.

care: No one should read this psalm and decide what is wrong with someone else. It does not say why he is low, and it gives no single cure. If ‘my tears have been my food both day and night’ is true of you now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Is there a song or a prayer from church that you still catch yourself humming?
discuss: The man in Psalm 42 remembers leading the crowds to God's house. Why might that memory hurt and help at the same time?
The psalm's refrain comes back more than once. What does it mean that hope sometimes has to be said again and again?
Is praying someone else's words a way of being honest, or a way of hiding? Why?
group.pray: Read Psalm 42 aloud together, slowly, a few verses each. Anyone may pass, and anyone may stop at a line they can't say.

sessions.title: When God seems silent
teaching: Sometimes faith doesn't end in an argument. It goes quiet. You pray, and nothing comes back, and after a while you stop. The Bible doesn't hide that silence. After his greatest day, the prophet Elijah ran into the wilderness and told God he had had enough, and God answered first with sleep, bread and water, and a second meal, before he asked Elijah a single question (1 Kings 19). Later, at the mountain, God was not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire. “And after the fire came a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12).

The page this session opens begins with a sentence worth keeping: feeling far from God is not the same as being far from him. Feelings rise and fall with sleep, grief and the weather. The page gives plain advice for a quiet season. Keep the practices when the warmth is gone, tell one honest believer where you are, and read the psalms of absence, written by people who felt exactly this and were not cast off. Jesus himself prayed the first line of one of them from the cross, and on the third day he was raised.

open.label: Feeling Far From God
open.why: Feeling far from God is not the same as being far from him: what Scripture says, and what to do while the feeling is quiet.

also.label: Why does God seem silent sometimes?
also.why: The psalms of complaint, Elijah under the tree and at the mountain, and the cry from the cross, in seven short pictures.

sessions.question: When did God last seem near to you, and what has changed since then: God, you, or what was happening around you?
sessions.do: Read 1 Kings 19:1-18 slowly and notice what God gives Elijah before he asks him anything. Then ask what you need this week before any answer: sleep, food, rest, or a friend.

verse.text: Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence? If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there.

care: If you feel forsaken right now and the feeling will not lift, please tell someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever been close to someone who went quiet for a long time? What did the silence feel like?
discuss: God gave Elijah sleep and food before he asked him anything. What does that say about how God treats a person at the end of their strength?
The page says feelings rise and fall with sleep, grief and the weather. How much of your sense of God's distance might be one of those?
Jesus prayed a psalm of abandonment from the cross. What does it mean that he knew this silence too?
group.pray: Those who pray may tell God honestly how far away he seems, and pray for anyone in the group in a long silence. Others can keep a minute of quiet.

sessions.title: Thrown out, and found
teaching: If you want to meet Jesus apart from the voice that misused him, read him for yourself. John 9 is a good place to start. Jesus heals a man born blind, and the religious authorities spend the rest of the chapter trying to make his story go away. Even his parents are afraid to stand with him. The man keeps telling the plain truth about what happened: “There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” (John 9:25). In the end the leaders tell him he was born in sin, and they throw him out.

Then comes the line to hold onto. “When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man” (John 9:35). Nobody else in the story goes looking for him. The notes on this chapter put it plainly: if you have been put out, by a church or a family or a town, remember that Jesus went looking for the man they threw out. The chapter ends with a warning, and it is aimed at the people who were sure they could see. The notes add that it reaches religious readers most of all.

open.label: John 9, passage by passage
open.why: A man healed, questioned, and thrown out by the religious leaders, and the one person in the story who goes looking for him.

sessions.question: What is the one thing you know for yourself about Jesus, even if you are unsure of everything else?
sessions.do: Read John 9 in one sitting, with the notes under the text. Write down each name the man gives Jesus as the chapter goes on, and notice how the names grow.

verse.text: When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man and said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”

care: A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever told the truth about something and been punished for it?
discuss: The disciples treat the blind man as a puzzle about who sinned. How does Jesus treat him instead?
The man's parents are afraid to stand with him. Why do people stay quiet when someone near them is pushed out?
The leaders were sure they could see. Where might a church, or any of us, be that sure today?
group.pray: Those who pray may give thanks that Jesus went looking for the man who was thrown out, and pray for anyone in the group put out of a church or a family. Others can keep a minute of quiet.

sessions.title: Do one thing he said
teaching: Faith that has come apart is not always rebuilt by argument. Some of it comes back by doing. Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders, and the wise one is “everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them” (Matthew 7:24). The sermon begins in Matthew 5 with the people Jesus calls fortunate in God's kingdom: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for what is right, the merciful, the peacemakers. It is not the list most people would have written.

Then come six sayings, each setting what was said before beside what Jesus says now: anger and contempt, desire, divorce, a word that can be trusted, the other cheek, and love for enemies. The notes on the chapter are careful. Refusing revenge still means keeping yourself and others safe, and praying for someone who wronged you is not excusing what they did. You don't have to settle what you believe before you try one of these. Choose one, do it this week, and notice what it does to you.

open.label: Matthew 5, passage by passage
open.why: The opening of the Sermon on the Mount in plain words: who is well off in God's kingdom, anger, enemies, and a yes that means yes.

sessions.question: Which of Jesus' sayings in Matthew 5 is hardest for you to hear, and which do you most wish the church had lived?
sessions.do: Read Matthew 5 to 7 in one sitting. Then choose one thing Jesus says to do, and do it this week: make peace with someone, give something away in secret, or pray by name for someone who wronged you.

verse.text: Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.

care: If you have been harmed by someone in a church, and were told to forgive and say nothing, what happened to you may have been wrong. Please talk with someone you trust outside that situation. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who is the kindest person you have known who never talked about it?
discuss: Jesus begins with the poor, the grieving and the hungry. Why might that list surprise people who have been in church a long time?
Which of the six sayings in Matthew 5 would change your week most if you did it?
Can a person act on Jesus' words before they are sure what they believe about him? What might happen if they did?
group.pray: Those who pray may ask for help to do one thing Jesus said this week, and pray for the people each person will act toward. Others can name their one thing in the quiet.

sessions.title: The faith before your church
teaching: The faith is older than any church you knew. The Apostles' Creed was not written by the apostles. It grew out of the questions put to new believers at their baptism in the second century: do you believe in God the Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, in the Holy Spirit? Over five centuries it settled into the form Western churches still say together. It is the oldest summary of Christian belief in continuous use, and it is short enough to learn in an afternoon.

Read it slowly and notice what it says. Maker of heaven and earth. Born of a woman with a name. Suffered under Pontius Pilate, a governor you can date. Crucified, dead and buried, and raised on the third day. Then notice what isn't there: no party, no dating rule, no style of worship, no timeline for the end of the world. Whatever you decide about Christianity, decide about this, and not only about the package it came in. It asks you to believe more than the package did, not less.

open.label: The Apostles' Creed
open.why: The oldest summary of the faith still in use, with notes on what each phrase was answering and why it was chosen.

sessions.question: Which lines of the creed can you say honestly today, which are you unsure of, and which can't you say?
sessions.do: Read the Apostles' Creed with its notes. Mark each line as one you believe, one you're not sure of, or one you don't. Keep the page, because the last session asks for it back.

verse.text: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Did you ever say a creed aloud in church? What do you remember of it?
discuss: The creed names Pontius Pilate. Why would a summary of the faith tie itself to a date in history?
What were you taught as if it were essential that the creed never mentions?
If the creed is the faith and the rest is the package, which part of the package was hardest to carry?
group.pray: Those who pray may give thanks for the people who handed this faith down, and ask for honesty about the lines they can't yet say. Others can read the creed in silence.

sessions.title: The longer story
teaching: The church you knew is one small part of a long story. It began with a few dozen followers of a crucified teacher in Jerusalem, and within a lifetime there were believers in Antioch, Corinth, Rome and Ephesus. They had no buildings, no salaried clergy, and no standing in the empire. The first lesson of the course this session opens asks what held them together before the New Testament was even gathered, and names four things: a short summary of the faith passed on by word of mouth, the worship every gathering shared, a line of trusted leaders, and the Spirit they believed lived among them.

The course is honest about the failures too: the crusades and the inquisition, the wars of religion, and the revival preachers who made their peace with slavery. It doesn't excuse any of them. But it also shows the faith outliving the people who misrepresented it, again and again, and being recovered by people who dug down to what was older. Seeing that can loosen the grip of one church's version. The faith did not begin with the people who hurt you, and it will not end with them.

open.label: Church history
open.why: Two thousand years on one line, and a course of lessons in order from the apostles to today, honest about the failures.

sessions.question: What would change for you if the church you knew turned out to be one chapter in a much longer story?
sessions.do: Read the first lesson of the course. Write down the four things it says held the first Christians together, and mark which of them your own church had and which it lacked.

verse.text: Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations.

group.open: How far back can you trace your own family's faith, or its lack of one?
discuss: The first Christians had no buildings and no standing in the empire. What does a church need, and what can it do without?
The course tells the church's failures plainly. Does that make the history easier to trust, or harder?
Which part of the church's story would you most like to understand, and why that part?
group.pray: Those who pray may give thanks for the people who carried the faith through hard centuries, and ask to see both the church's failures and its gifts honestly. Others can keep a minute of quiet.

sessions.title: The question you couldn't ask
teaching: Many people step back because of a question they were never allowed to ask. It might have been hell, or the violence in the Old Testament, or whether the Gospels can be trusted, or why a good God allows so much suffering. Maybe you asked once and got a verse and a warning instead of an answer. A question treated as disloyalty doesn't go away. It goes underground, and it grows there, unanswered, until it carries more weight than anything else you were taught.

The library this session opens takes hard questions one at a time, in ten areas, from the arguments for God to the church's own record. Each piece states the objection at its strongest and says what is true in it. Then it sets out the evidence and the argument, gives the best reply it can, and names what remains unresolved and where Christians themselves differ. You may not be persuaded by every answer. But you will find your question asked honestly, by people who expected it to be asked.

open.label: The case for the faith
open.why: Hard questions taken one at a time: the objection at its strongest, what is true in it, the evidence, and what remains unresolved.

also.label: For skeptics
also.why: If your question is whether any of it is true at all, this room lays out the case step by step, at your own pace.

sessions.question: What is the question you were never allowed to ask, and what would count as an honest answer to it?
sessions.do: Write that question down in one sentence. Find it, or the one nearest to it, in the library, read the piece to the end, and note where you would push back.

verse.text: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.

group.open: What question did you ask as a child or a teenager that nobody answered?
discuss: Why do you think some churches treat a question as disloyalty?
Each piece in the library names what remains unresolved. Does that make it more trustworthy to you, or less?
What would you need from the person you asked your hardest question?
group.pray: Those who pray may bring their hardest question to God just as it is, and pray for patience with one another's questions. Others can sit with their own question in the quiet.

sessions.title: What comes after
teaching: A track like this can't tell you where to land, and it won't try. But the answer this session opens names something worth facing. Taking apart what deserves it is honest, and sometimes it is closer to repentance than to rebellion. Doubt by itself, though, builds nothing. Suspicion can tell you what to tear down, but it can't tell you how to live on an ordinary Tuesday, and a cleared field doesn't stay empty for long. Something always moves in.

Jesus could be relentless with the religious leaders of his day, but his demolition always had a destination. So the question at the end of these sessions is not whether you have finished. It is whether you are digging toward something, and not only away. A father once came to Jesus with a son in danger and a faith he wasn't sure of, and his prayer is one of the shortest in the Bible: “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus didn't send him away to get his certainty in order first. You can take as long as you need, and you don't have to take it alone.

open.label: What happens after deconstruction?
open.why: Why taking apart what deserves it is honest, and the question that follows: whether you are tearing toward anything and not only away.

also.label: Eight Weeks of Taking Your Questions Seriously
also.why: If you want company for the questions: eight weeks from sorting what you were handed down to the older faith underneath, at your own pace.

also.label: I'm not sure I believe anymore
also.why: If you used to be sure and now you aren't: what doubt is and isn't, what Scripture says to people who doubt, and what to do this week.

sessions.question: Looking back over these sessions, what are you taking apart, and what, if anything, are you digging toward?
sessions.do: Take out the creed you marked in session 9 and read it again. Then choose one next step and begin it: the eight-week plan, a Gospel read slowly, or one honest conversation with a believer you trust.

verse.text: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

care: If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Since the first session, what has changed, if anything, in how you think about God, the church, or yourself?
discuss: The answer says a cleared field doesn't stay empty for long. What has moved into the space where your faith used to be?
What is the difference between tearing down toward something and tearing down only to get away?
The father in Mark 9 believed and doubted in a single breath. Is that a prayer you could pray?
group.pray: Those who pray may thank God by name for each person in the group and for every honest question asked, and ask rest for each one. Others can keep a minute of quiet.
